newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Israel says U.N. Mideast session would be "sterile".
newsitem.headline: Israel says U.N. Mideast session would be "sterile".

text.p: Israeli U.N. envoy David Peleg said on Wednesday an emergency special session of the General Assembly requested by Arab states on the issue of Israeli settlements would only prove sterile and a source of further polarisation.
"Only direct negotiations between the sides can bring about reconciliation," he told reporters.

Noting the issue had been debated twice last month by the Security Council and once by the Assembly, he said: "We definitely feel that another session can only prove sterile...it would become a source of further polarisation."
The Palestine Liberation Organisation's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, said later he hoped the emergency special session of the Assembly would be convened next week.

A resolution still being drafted would include a recommendation for "collective measures on behalf of the international community," he added, but did not spell out what form those measures might take.

The 22-member Arab group has asked for the Assembly session under a 1950 "uniting for peace" formula that enables issues to be dealt with by the Assembly when vetoes prevent the Security Council from acting.

The United States, on March 7 and again on March 21, vetoed Security Council resolutions calling on Israel to halt the building of 6,500 homes for Jews on a site between Jerusalem and Bethlehem captured during the 1967 Middle East war. It is called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew.

The General Assembly, at a resumed session last month, adopted a resolution by a vote of 130 to two, with two abstentions, calling on Israel to abandon the project. There is no veto in the Assembly, whose decisions are not binding.

Peleg said recent Arab initiatives, including calls by a foreign ministers' meeting in Cairo for a freeze in relations with Israel and a resumption of the Arab economic boycott, seemed intended to "turn the clock back and bring the area back to the era before the Madrid peace conference" which launched the peace process in 1991.

He also said it was vital for Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and the Palestinian Authority "to take clear steps against terrorism to enable the resumption of the talks between us and the Palestinians on all levels, including the level of Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu and Chairman Arafat."
He was referring to the March 21 suicide bombing of a Tel Aviv cafe in which three Israelis were killed and many wounded, and other recent violent incidents.

Al-Kidwa said the resolution to be submitted to the Assembly would "reiterate the basic positions of the United Nations with regard to illegal Israeli actions, particularly those related to Jerusalem and...settlement activities," and express support for the peace process and the full and immediate implementation of agreements.
It would also "have a practical aspect through which the General Assembly could recommend collective measures on behalf of the international community," he said.

Asked whether he wanted a special mission sent to the occupied territories, al-Kidwa replied: "This is a possibility. There is a possibility of having some kind of a U.N. mechanism. There is another kind of possibility of having a mechanism to be dealt with by member states directly."
Referring to Israeli settlements, he said: "While we are ready to negotiate...political confrontation with the Israeli side will continue as long as illegal Israeli actions continue."
